newsitem.title: GERMANY: German CDU members mull new tax moves - report.
newsitem.headline: German CDU members mull new tax moves - report.

text.p: Leading politicians from German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) on Saturday called for a rise in a wide range of indirect taxes in order to finance income tax cuts and the ailing pension system.

The demands come just days after the government presented a sharply-criticised income tax reform that envisages tax cuts of 82 billion marks to be financed by scrapping tax breaks and raising value-added taxes.

But now leading CDU politicians want to raise other taxes such as petrol, tobacco and spirits in order to ensure a planned reform of pension insurance will not contain hidden payments to finance the income tax cuts.

Labour Minister Norbert Bluem, expected to present a pension reform plan to cabinet next week, said he would only do so if it were clear from the start that payments that had nothing to do with financing pensions were not included.
"This has to be cleared up," he told the weekly Bild am Sonntag newspaper in an interview to be published on Sunday.
"It is now or never. I will not present a reform without an answer to the question what taxpayers and people paying into pension plans will have to pay for in the future."
Bluem got immediate support from CDU general secretary Peter Hintze.

"We will quickly present a concept that secures future pensions and creates the relationship between the tax system and the pension system as desired by Norbert Bluem," Hintze told a CDU state party congress in eastern Brandenburg state.
Bluem wants services that are not related to pensions that were previously financed by pension payments to be funded in future by the tax system.

Michael Glos, parliamentary leader of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's sister party in their centre-right coalition with the liberal Free Democrats, suggested raising some taxes as compensation.
"One way would be to close the gap with other indirect taxes," he told the weekly news magazine Der Spiegel in an article released ahead of publication on Monday.
The Association of German Pension Insurers (VDR), grouping state pension funds, criticised the government's plans to tax pension payments.
Franz Ruland, VDR managing director, told the Mainz daily Allegemeine Zeitung that the relationship between what is paid into pension funds and the services received was steadily deteriorating.
"Monthly payments are rising, the retirement age is to be raised, the general level should be lowered and all of this is combined with heavy taxation of pensions," he complained.
